title: 2026 Toyota Tundra Hybrid: Prices, Reviews & Pictures - CarGurus.com
summary: Explore the 2026 Toyota Tundra Hybrid with CarGurus reviews, pricing insights, comparisons, news and expert analysis.
body_markdown:
## Look & feel


8/10


The exterior design of the Toyota Tundra Hybrid can be polarizing with its blocky wheel arches, hard horizontal lines, and inverted, U-shaped mustache grille, but observers cannot mistake it for any other truck on the road. And the styling has grown on us over the past four years. We like the grille and wheel designs keyed to different trim levels, which give each grade its own personality from functional to fancy. This individualization transfers to the interior with different materials, dash designs, and stitching accents based on trim.


Our test truck this time around was the TRD Pro, but we’ve previously had access to the Limited, Platinum, 1794 Edition, and Capstone models, and even though each interior looks different, the overall fit-and-finish is well done throughout the lineup. On the TRD Pro test truck, the blocky TOYOTA lettering on the dash and camouflaged pattern on the leatherette seats gave it a modern but rugged vibe. On the top-tier Capstone, buyers get two-tone leather on the dash with more premium-looking accents and materials throughout. All hybrid trims come with a 14-inch infotainment screen that looks like a large tablet affixed to the center of the dash. But we appreciate that even with such a large screen, there are still hard-touch buttons and dials for the climate control and audio volume.


While the non-hybrids have multiple cab and bed configurations as well as more basic work truck models, Tundra Hybrid trims start at the Limited grade. The only cab option is the four-door CrewMax, but the Limited, Platinum, and 1794 Edition offer both 5.5-foot and 6.5-foot bed options. The TRD Pro and Capstone only come with the 5.5-foot bed option.


## Performance


8/10


The Tundra Hybrid comes with Toyota's i-Force Max powertrain, consisting of a twin-turbo V6 and a single electric motor generator that sits between the engine and the 10-speed automatic transmission. This setup provides instantaneous torque, which eliminates turbo lag and provides smooth, fast acceleration. Total system output is 437 horsepower and 583 pound-feet of torque.


As a full-size truck, the Tundra Hybrid is by no means nimble, but during a 400-mile road trip between Chicago and Iowa, we found it had plenty of oomph for passing and merging maneuvers on the highway. The driver’s seat was comfortable for the long haul, with a good position for most people. However, drivers on the petite side might have more blind spots due to the truck’s high belt line.


At city speeds, we found the Tundra Hybrid to be quiet thanks to its primarily electric operation, and it smoothed out the worst of the potholes and speed bumps. On the highway, though, we found ourselves cranking up the volume on our podcasts to be able to hear the conversation over the knobby all-terrain tires and the sound of the engine. And when we took a couple of phone calls, we felt as though we were shouting at the people on the other end of the line.


While we didn’t have the opportunity to tow during this test period, we can say from previous experience that the Tundra Hybrid still manages to be peppy even when carrying a load. The powertrain is so good that drivers hardly feel the weight of what’s behind them. While the Tundra Hybrid has a maximum towing capacity of 11,450 pounds (in the Limited 4X2 trim) that’s less than every other full-size truck, there is a certain smoothness that makes a big difference.


## Form & function


7/10


There is only one cab configuration, but the choice of two bed lengths is appreciated. The Tundra’s bed is made from Sheet-Molded Composite (SMC) with aluminum reinforcement, so there's no need for a spray-in bed liner or to worry about the rust or dent issues of a conventional steel bed. Other great features include a 120-volt in-bed power outlet, a deck rail system with cargo tie-downs, LED bed lighting, and a power tailgate with knee-lift assist.


The cab offers great stowage spaces, from the large console bin under the armrest to the illuminated glove box, to the sunglasses storage in the overhead console. Six cup holders and four bottle holders provide plenty of beverage space. However, unlike non-hybrid versions of the Tundra, there’s no under-seat storage in the back because the space is taken up by the hybrid system’s battery pack. Storage pockets on the backs of the front seats for smaller items are as good as it gets.


Other favorite convenience features of ours include the power running boards (standard on the Capstone), heated and ventilated front seats, and the power rear window that lowers entirely.


## Technology


8/10


Since the Tundra Hybrid starts at the Limited trim, buyers get more standard features than they would with a base non-hybrid Tundra. The hybrid comes standard with a 14-inch infotainment screen, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, a nine-speaker audio system, a 12.3-inch digital cluster, dual-zone automatic climate control, and five USB ports. Available features include a head-up display, a 12-speaker JBL audio system, and wireless phone charging.


Standard towing kit includes a Tow/Haul drive mode and trailer sway control. Available features include an LED trailering light and a trailer backup guide system.


Throughout the test period, all the technology worked as it should. We loved the wireless Apple CarPlay as well as the native infotainment system, which made it easy to switch from podcasts to phone calls to apps.


## Safety


9/10


The 2026 Toyota Tundra CrewCab is one of the only full-size pickup trucks to receive an Insurance Institute for Highway Safety Top Safety Pick award with Good crashworthiness scores and a mix of Good and Acceptable scores for crash avoidance, seat belts, and child restraints. The only other truck that scored better is the all-electric Tesla Cybertruck; none of the Detroit Three trucks received a Top Safety Pick designation. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration gave the Tundra Hybrid a five-out-of-five-star overall safety rating.


The Tundra Hybrid also offers lots of standard driver-assistance tech, including adaptive cruise control, automatic emergency braking with pedestrian detection, lane-departure warning with steering assist, lane-centering assist, high-beam assist, traffic-sign recognition, blind-spot monitors (with trailer coverage), rear cross-traffic alert, and tire-pressure monitoring. A surround-view camera system and rearview camera mirror are also available.


Other safety features include eight airbags and a LATCH system with lower anchors on all outboard second-row seats. A complimentary 10-year subscription to Safety Connect is standard, too, which includes emergency assistance, a stolen vehicle locator, roadside assistance, and automatic collision notification.


## Cost-effectiveness


7/10


The Tundra Hybrid has a higher base price than the Ford F-150 PowerBoost, which is the only other full-size truck available with a hybrid powertrain. The base F-150 hybrid trim level, the STX, is about $5,000 less than the base Tundra Hybrid Limited, but it doesn’t have leather upholstery, power front seats with heating and ventilation, dual-zone climate control, adaptive cruise control, or front and rear parking sensors. The more comparable F-150 trim is the Lariat, which costs about $8,000 more than the Tundra Hybrid Limited.


The F-150 PowerBoost has a slightly higher maximum towing capacity (11,600 pounds vs. 11,450 pounds) and maximum payload (1,740 pounds vs. 1,655 pounds). The Ford also has a higher combined fuel economy of 23 mpg vs. 20 mpg for the Toyota, but the Toyota has more horsepower (+7 hp) and more torque (+13 lb-ft) than the Ford.


For the highest mpg and the lowest price of entry, the Ford F-150 PowerBoost is the better option. But for more power, more creature comforts, and better safety ratings, the Tundra is the truck buyers want.


We’d stick with the well-equipped base Limited trim, but add four-wheel drive (4WD, $3,000) and the Limited PVM (panoramic view monitor) Package ($950), bringing the total price to $64,705 with the $2,195 destination fee. This adds a boatload of premium amenities, extra traction for inclement weather, and extra camera views for parallel parking or tight city spaces.
